questions.questionText: What is the primary characteristic of a pretexting attack?

options.text: Bombarding a website with fake internet traffic.
Fabricating a scenario and identity to build trust and trick a victim into sharing data.
Infecting USB drives left in public parking lots.
Sending mass generic spam to millions of emails.

questions.explanation: Pretexting centers on creating a plausible false persona and narrative.

questions.questionText: Pretexting attacks always happen within a single 30-second interaction and never involve multi-day conversations.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Pretexting often uses a "slow-burn" approach, building rapport across multiple days or weeks.

questions.questionText: Someone claiming to be an "External ISO Auditor" contacts a remote worker asking for a complete list of internal server IP addresses. The caller says opening an IT ticket will take too long. What should the worker do?

options.text: Email the server IP list immediately.
Insist on routing the request through official internal ticketing and manager approval channels.
Post the server IP addresses on social media.
Give the auditor their home Wi-Fi password.

questions.explanation: Never bypass formal verification and ticketing procedures for external inquiries.

questions.questionText: Why do pretexters often try to discourage victims from submitting official IT service tickets?

options.text: IT tickets cost money to create.
Official tickets trigger administrative logs and security reviews that would expose the fake identity.
IT ticketing systems automatically block phone calls.
Scammers prefer using postal mail.

questions.explanation: Formal ticketing creates an audit trail that alerts legitimate security personnel.

questions.questionText: Which of the following personas are common disguises used in pretexting campaigns? *(Select TWO)*

options.text: An external compliance auditor conducting an "urgent audit."
A distressed remote contractor needing file access due to an "emergency."
An automated operating system update wizard.
A physical hardware firewall appliance.

questions.explanation: Pretexters assume roles that invoke authority (auditor) or empathy (distressed colleague).

questions.questionText: Pretexting relies heavily on human psychological traits like helpfulness, politeness, and respect for authority.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Attackers exploit natural human social tendencies to manipulate targets.

questions.questionText: You receive a message from a "new vendor" asking for internal directory structures so they can "prepare project integration." You have not received any notification from management about a new vendor. What is the correct protocol?

options.text: Send the directory file immediately.
Do not share internal data; verify the vendor’s onboarding status with your internal manager or procurement team.
Ask the vendor to pay you $50.
Send them dummy data containing real employee passwords.

questions.explanation: Unverified third parties must be vetted through management before receiving internal assets.

questions.questionText: How does pretexting differ from mass phishing?

options.text: Pretexting uses malicious email attachments exclusively.
Pretexting focuses on building a credible narrative and relationship, whereas mass phishing relies on broad, generic lures.
Mass phishing only targets phone landlines.
Pretexting is legally permitted in business.

questions.explanation: Pretexting prioritizes narrative depth and trust over volume.

questions.questionText: A pretexter will never use public information from LinkedIn to build their fake story.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Pretexters extensively use OSINT from LinkedIn and company sites to make their scenarios believable.

questions.questionText: What term describes an attacker engaging a victim in casual conversation over several days to establish a sense of normal friendship before executing a scam?

options.text: Buffer Overflow
Trust-Building / Slow-Burn Pretexting
Man-in-the-Middle
Zero-Day Exploit

questions.explanation: Slow-burn pretexting grooms the victim over time to lower security vigilance.

questions.questionText: A remote contractor receives an email from someone claiming to be "Head of Global Security": *"We are running a silent security exercise. Do not inform your supervisor. Send your current VPN credentials directly to this email."* What should the contractor do?

options.text: Follow instructions and keep quiet.
Ignore the secrecy request and immediately report the message to their official supervisor and security team.
Reply asking for a cash reward.
Post the VPN credentials on an online forum.

questions.explanation: Demands for secrecy and credential submission are major red flags; legitimate security exercises do not collect user passwords via email.

questions.questionText: What structural control prevents pretexting attempts from compromising internal resources?

options.text: Allowing employees to share passwords freely.
Enforcing strict adherence to official identity verification and ticketing channels.
Removing password locks from work laptops.
Disabling all antivirus software.

questions.explanation: Formal channels and strict verification neutralize pretexting narratives.

questions.questionText: Pretexters never target remote workers who do not have executive titles.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Administrative assistants, support staff, and contractors are frequently targeted for their access to directory data and internal processes.

questions.questionText: Which conversational signs suggest an interaction may be a pretexting attempt? *(Select TWO)*

options.text: The contact asks for confidential data while insisting you skip standard manager approval.
The contact uses an elaborate, emotional story to justify an unusual information request.
The contact directs you to submit a ticket through the official company portal.
The contact's identity is verified by your department manager in person.

questions.explanation: Bypassing procedures and using high-emotion stories are common pretexting tactics.

questions.questionText: What should you do if an external party claiming to be an auditor asks for employee home addresses?

options.text: Send the addresses in a plain text file.
Refuse and escalate the inquiry to your company's official legal or HR department.
Ask for $10 per address.
Guess the addresses and send random data.

questions.explanation: Personally Identifiable Information (PII) disclosures must be handled exclusively by authorized departments.

questions.questionText: Pretexting can occur over email, phone calls, social media, or messaging apps.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Pretexting is medium-agnostic and occurs across any communication channel.

questions.questionText: A remote worker receives a call from an individual claiming to be a printer technician needing internal Wi-Fi passwords to fix an office printer 500 miles away. Why is this request suspicious?

options.text: Printers do not use electricity.
The scenario lacks logical plausibility, and Wi-Fi credentials should never be shared verbally with external technicians.
Technicians only speak French.
Wi-Fi passwords cannot be typed on laptops.

questions.explanation: Evaluating the logical plausibility of a request helps spot flawed pretexts.

questions.questionText: What role does flattery play in pretexting interactions?

options.text: It encrypts the user's hard drive.
It lowers the victim's defenses by making them feel valued and eager to assist.
It speeds up internet connection bandwidth.
It triggers automated firewall logging.

questions.explanation: Flattery creates positive rapport, encouraging the target to comply with requests.

questions.questionText: Out-of-band verification is ineffective against pretexting.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Independent out-of-band verification effectively exposes pretexts by contacting the real organization or individual.

questions.questionText: What is the gold standard rule when handling requests for sensitive corporate information?

options.text: Share the data if the caller sounds friendly.
Verify identity and authorization through official channels before releasing any data.
Always post data on public forums.
Never talk to anyone at work.

questions.explanation: Always verify identity and clearance before transmitting sensitive data. MODULE 6: Essential Safe Practices for Remote Env
